project.name: MAPD-B
project.description: Hands-on lecture materials for the Management and Analysis of Physics Datasets - Module B (MAPD-B) course, M.Sc. in Physics of Data, University of Padova (2025-2026). Organized by topic into Jupyter notebooks and Python scripts covering MySQL, parallel programming, Apache Spark, Dask, and Apache Kafka, each with its own Docker Compose setup.

nodes.name: 00_single_threaded.py
nodes.summary: Baseline script that sums a large range of integers single-threaded and times the execution, used as a performance reference point before introducing threading.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b) in a simple loop and prints the result.

nodes.name: 01_multi_threaded.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates basic Python multithreading by splitting the same summation workload across two Thread instances running the shared my_sum function concurrently, with start/join semantics explained in comments.
nodes.languageNotes: Illustrates non-blocking thread.start() versus blocking thread.join() semantics in Python's threading module.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b) and prints the result; invoked concurrently by two threads splitting the workload in half.

nodes.name: 02_multi_threaded_local_data.py
nodes.summary: Variant of the multithreaded summation example that introduces threading.local() to illustrate (and contrast against) explicit thread-local storage, though the accumulator is still a plain local variable in practice.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b), initializing a threading.local() instance to demonstrate thread-local memory before falling back to a plain per-call accumulator.

nodes.name: 03_multi_threaded_nolock.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates a race condition by having two threads concurrently mutate shared global state (COMMON_COUNTER and COMMON_LIST) without synchronization, then cross-checks and highlights the resulting inconsistency in red using colorama.
nodes.languageNotes: Classic unsynchronized shared-state mutation across threads producing a race condition, verified by comparing COMMON_COUNTER against len(COMMON_LIST).

nodes.name: my_sum_mod
nodes.summary: Sums integers in [a, b) while unsynchronized-mutating shared globals COMMON_COUNTER and COMMON_LIST whenever a value is a multiple of m, exposing a race condition across concurrent threads.

nodes.name: 03extra_minimal_race_condition.py
nodes.summary: Minimal reproducible race condition example spawning 10 threads that all increment a shared global counter without locking, typically producing a final value less than the expected 10,000,000 due to lost updates.
nodes.languageNotes: Compact demonstration that Python's GIL does not make compound operations like `counter += 1` atomic across threads.

nodes.name: increment
nodes.summary: Increments a shared global counter max_val times without synchronization, used as the target function for 10 concurrent threads to expose a race condition.

nodes.name: 04_multi_threaded_lock.py
nodes.summary: Fixes the race condition from the nolock example by wrapping the shared-state mutation of COMMON_COUNTER and COMMON_LIST in a threading.Lock acquire/release pair, guaranteeing consistent results across concurrent threads.
nodes.languageNotes: Demonstrates mutual exclusion via threading.Lock to serialize access to a critical section shared across threads, eliminating the race condition shown in 03_multi_threaded_nolock.py.

nodes.name: my_sum_mod
nodes.summary: Sums integers in [a, b) while safely mutating shared globals COMMON_COUNTER and COMMON_LIST inside a lock-protected critical section whenever a value is a multiple of m.

nodes.name: 04extra_minimal_race_condition_with_lock.py
nodes.summary: Minimal demonstration of a race condition fix using threading.Lock, where 10 threads increment a shared global counter safely inside a critical section.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses a module-level global counter and a threading.Lock acquired/released around the critical section to serialize access across 10 concurrent threads.

nodes.name: increment
nodes.summary: Increments a shared global counter max_val times, guarding each increment with a lock acquire/release to avoid a race condition.

nodes.name: 05_multi_threaded_pool_lock.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates ThreadPoolExecutor with a shared Lock to safely aggregate a common counter and list while four threads each sum a partition of a large range.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor and wait() to collect futures; a shared Lock protects COMMON_COUNTER and COMMON_LIST mutated from multiple threads.

nodes.name: my_sum_mod
nodes.summary: Sums integers in [a, b) and, for multiples of m, safely updates a shared counter and list under a lock; returns the partial sum.

nodes.name: 06_multi_threaded_pool_queue.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates ThreadPoolExecutor combined with a thread-safe queue.Queue as an alternative to explicit locking for collecting values found by concurrent worker threads.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses queue.Queue.put()/get() as an inherently thread-safe structure, avoiding the need for a manual Lock used in the sibling 05_ script.

nodes.name: my_sum_mod
nodes.summary: Sums integers in [a, b) and pushes multiples of m onto a shared thread-safe queue instead of using a lock; returns the partial sum.

nodes.name: 07_multi_processing.py
nodes.summary: Basic example of true parallelism using multiprocessing.Process, spawning two separate OS processes that each sum half of a large integer range concurrently.
nodes.languageNotes: Uses multiprocessing.Process.start()/join() directly rather than a pool, illustrating the most basic sub-process API and bypassing the GIL entirely.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b) and prints the result; used as the target function for each spawned process.

nodes.name: 08_multi_processing_pool_starmap.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates multiprocessing.Pool.starmap to distribute a range-sum computation across 4 worker processes with a blocking call that returns all results at once.
nodes.languageNotes: starmap is a blocking pool API that unpacks tuples of arguments into the target function, contrasting with the non-blocking starmap_async used in script 09.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b), prints, and returns the result; distributed across a process pool via starmap.

nodes.name: 09_multi_processing_pool_starmapasync.py
nodes.summary: Demonstrates the non-blocking multiprocessing.Pool.starmap_async API, polling readiness in a loop while sub-processes compute partial sums in the background.
nodes.languageNotes: starmap_async returns immediately and exposes .ready()/.get(), letting the main thread continue other work until results are needed, unlike the blocking starmap in script 08.

nodes.name: my_sum
nodes.summary: Sums integers in the range [a, b), prints, and returns the result; distributed asynchronously across a process pool via starmap_async.

nodes.name: cpu_intensive.py
nodes.summary: Sequential baseline for a CPU-bound Monte Carlo integration benchmark, running 10 chunks of a numerical integration one after another without any concurrency.
nodes.languageNotes: Serves as the timing baseline compared against the threaded and multiprocessing variants of the same computation, useful for illustrating the GIL's effect on CPU-bound workloads.

nodes.name: f
nodes.summary: Arbitrary mathematical function sin(1/(x*(2-x)))^2 used as the integrand for the Monte Carlo integration.

nodes.name: cpu_function
nodes.summary: Performs a seeded Monte Carlo integration of f(x) over 2 million random samples and returns the hit count and sample size.

nodes.name: cpu_intensive_threading.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same CPU-bound Monte Carlo integration as cpu_intensive.py but distributes the 10 chunks across a ThreadPoolExecutor, illustrating that threading provides no speedup for CPU-bound work due to the GIL.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to cpu_intensive.py and cpu_intensive_multiprocessing.py to contrast sequential, threaded, and multi-process execution times for the same CPU-bound task.

nodes.name: f
nodes.summary: Arbitrary mathematical function sin(1/(x*(2-x)))^2 used as the integrand for the Monte Carlo integration.

nodes.name: cpu_function
nodes.summary: Performs a seeded Monte Carlo integration of f(x) over 2 million random samples and returns the hit count and sample size; submitted as a task to a ThreadPoolExecutor.

nodes.name: cpu_intensive_multiprocessing.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same CPU-bound Monte Carlo integration as cpu_intensive.py but distributes the 10 chunks across separate processes, demonstrating real parallel speedup for CPU-bound work by bypassing the GIL.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to cpu_intensive.py and cpu_intensive_threading.py; multiprocessing achieves true parallelism for CPU-bound tasks where threading cannot due to the GIL.

nodes.name: f
nodes.summary: Arbitrary mathematical function sin(1/(x*(2-x)))^2 used as the integrand for the Monte Carlo integration.

nodes.name: cpu_function
nodes.summary: Performs a seeded Monte Carlo integration of f(x) over 2 million random samples and returns the hit count and sample size; distributed across worker processes.

nodes.name: io_intensive.py
nodes.summary: Sequential baseline for an I/O-bound benchmark that downloads a list of remote image URLs one at a time and saves each to disk under a content-hashed filename.
nodes.languageNotes: Serves as the timing baseline compared against the threaded and multiprocessing I/O variants, illustrating that threading (unlike for CPU-bound work) does help I/O-bound workloads since the GIL is released during blocking I/O.

nodes.name: io_intensive_threading.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same I/O-bound URL-fetching benchmark as io_intensive.py but distributes the downloads across a ThreadPoolExecutor, showing that threading speeds up I/O-bound work because the GIL is released during blocking network calls.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to io_intensive.py and io_intensive_multiprocessing.py to contrast sequential, threaded, and multi-process execution times for the same I/O-bound task.

nodes.name: io_function
nodes.summary: Fetches a remote file over HTTP, computes an MD5 hash of its content for the filename, and writes the file to the local pics directory; submitted as a task to a ThreadPoolExecutor.

nodes.name: io_intensive_multiprocessing.py
nodes.summary: Runs the same I/O-bound URL-fetching benchmark as io_intensive.py but distributes the downloads across separate processes, used to compare process-based vs thread-based vs sequential I/O concurrency.
nodes.languageNotes: Directly comparable to io_intensive.py and io_intensive_threading.py; for I/O-bound tasks, multiprocessing typically offers no advantage over threading but carries higher process-creation overhead.

nodes.name: io_function
nodes.summary: Fetches a remote file over HTTP, computes an MD5 hash of its content for the filename, and writes the file to the local pics directory; distributed across worker processes.

tour.title: Course Overview
tour.description: The root README is the course syllabus in miniature: a single table mapping five topic folders (mysql, parallel, spark, dask, kafka) to their subject areas. This is a hands-on lecture repository for the MAPD-B course at the University of Padova, not a single deployable application, so the 'architecture' here is really a curriculum -- each folder is a self-contained module with its own Docker environment and notebooks. The tour follows a learning path through these modules rather than a dependency graph.

tour.title: Parallel Programming Fundamentals
tour.description: Before touching any distributed-computing framework, the course grounds students in single-machine concurrency using pure Python and no Docker at all. The parallel/README.md explains the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), how to install multiple Python versions via deadsnakes, and tools like htop and taskset for observing CPU usage -- concepts that explain why Spark, Dask, and Kafka exist in the first place (a single Python process can't use multiple cores for CPU-bound work without extra machinery).

tour.title: Threads and the Race Condition
tour.description: The module builds up in small, deliberate steps: 00_single_threaded.py times a plain sequential sum as a baseline, 01_multi_threaded.py splits the same workload across two Thread objects to show basic start/join semantics, and 03_multi_threaded_nolock.py deliberately breaks correctness by having threads mutate shared global state without synchronization. Running these in order reproduces the classic 'threads look like free parallelism until they aren't' lesson -- 04_multi_threaded_lock.py then fixes the same race condition with a threading.Lock, and 03extra/04extra provide a minimal 10-thread counter example of the same bug and fix in isolation.
tour.languageLesson: Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) means only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time, so threading.Thread gives concurrency, not parallelism, for CPU-bound code. A threading.Lock's acquire/release pair creates a critical section: without it, 'increment the counter' is not atomic and concurrent threads can silently lose updates.

tour.title: CPU-Bound vs I/O-Bound: Threads, Processes, Pools
tour.description: Building on the lock/queue patterns from Step 3 (05_multi_threaded_pool_lock.py and 06_multi_threaded_pool_queue.py show ThreadPoolExecutor combined with a Lock or a thread-safe Queue), the module then contrasts two benchmark pairs that make the GIL's real-world impact concrete. cpu_intensive.py vs cpu_intensive_threading.py vs cpu_intensive_multiprocessing.py show that threading gives no speedup for CPU-bound Monte Carlo integration (the GIL blocks it) while multiprocessing does, and io_intensive.py vs its threading/multiprocessing variants show the opposite: threading helps I/O-bound work because the GIL is released during blocking network calls.
tour.languageLesson: multiprocessing.Process/Pool sidesteps the GIL entirely by running separate OS processes, each with its own Python interpreter and memory space -- the right tool for CPU-bound work. ThreadPoolExecutor is the right tool for I/O-bound work because blocking calls like network I/O release the GIL, letting other threads run while one waits.

tour.title: MySQL Module: Relational Databases
tour.description: With single-machine concurrency covered, the course moves to the simplest infrastructure module: a two-container stack (MySQL server plus a custom Jupyter client) for teaching SQL against the IMDb dataset. The mysql/README.md documents the startup/shutdown flow and the prerequisite of downloading the IMDb_pruned.sql dump, while mapd_notebook.Dockerfile shows how the Jupyter client image is built on python:3.14.2-slim with SQLAlchemy, ipython-sql, and mysql-connector-python. MySQL.ipynb is the introductory lecture notebook, connecting to the container and running basic SQL queries, with MySQL_solutions.ipynb as the optional worked-solutions companion.
tour.languageLesson: Multi-container Docker Compose stacks let a lecture bind a database server and a client tool together with one command, while a bind-mounted workspace volume means notebook edits persist outside the container. Building a custom client image (rather than using MySQL's own image for Jupyter) lets the course pin exact Python library versions (SQLAlchemy, ipython-sql) needed for the exercises.

tour.title: Spark Module: Distributed Computing Cluster
tour.description: The course's core distributed-computing unit introduces a real multi-node cluster: spark/docker-compose.yml defines a spark-master (resource manager, port 8080/7077), one or more scalable spark-worker replicas, and a jupyter-notebook service that bundles the Spark client and exposes both the notebook UI and the Spark application UI (port 4040). Unlike the single-container MySQL setup from Step 5, this is the first module where the docker-compose.yml itself models internal service dependencies (worker and notebook both depend_on the master), foreshadowing the cluster topology that Kafka's module reuses in Step 8.
tour.languageLesson: The Spark master/worker/driver model: the master tracks cluster resources, workers execute tasks, and the driver (running inside the Jupyter client here) submits jobs and coordinates execution. Docker Compose's depends_on and shared network let the driver discover spark-master by service name rather than a hardcoded IP.

tour.title: PySpark: RDDs to DataFrames to Streaming
tour.description: The three Spark lectures build directly on the cluster from Step 6 and escalate in abstraction. Lecture1.ipynb covers the low-level RDD API (parallelize, map, reduce) plus word count and Monte Carlo pi estimation; Lecture2.ipynb moves to the higher-level DataFrame/Spark SQL API with UDFs and Pandas UDFs; Lecture3.ipynb introduces Structured Streaming, reading a live TCP socket stream generated by producer.py and applying the same DataFrame operations to unbounded data. Each lecture has a solutions notebook as an optional companion for checking worked answers.
tour.languageLesson: RDDs (Resilient Distributed Datasets) are Spark's original low-level, partition-aware collection abstraction; DataFrames add a schema and a query optimizer (Catalyst) on top, usually performing better for structured data. Structured Streaming reuses the DataFrame API for unbounded data by treating a stream as a table that is continuously appended to.

tour.title: Kafka Module: Event Streaming on Top of Spark
tour.description: The Kafka module directly extends the Spark cluster pattern from Steps 6-7: kafka/docker-compose.yml combines the same Spark master/worker/Jupyter topology with a single-node Kafka broker running in KRaft mode (no separate Zookeeper needed, simplifying the stack). The kafka/README.md documents this combined cluster and outlines the lecture sequence: topics, producer/consumer APIs, consumer groups, and finally Spark Structured Streaming ingestion from Kafka -- explicitly bridging back to the streaming concepts introduced in Step 7's Lecture3.
tour.languageLesson: Kafka's KRaft mode replaces the older ZooKeeper-based metadata management with a built-in Raft consensus protocol, simplifying single-broker educational setups. Combining Kafka and Spark in one Compose stack lets the notebook client act as both a Kafka producer/consumer and a Spark Structured Streaming driver.

tour.title: Kafka Producer, Consumer, and Consumer Groups
tour.description: The Kafka lectures follow the publish/subscribe model end to end. Producer.ipynb shows publishing messages first from the broker's own shell, then via the Python kafka-python client; Consumer.ipynb shows instantiating a KafkaConsumer and subscribing to topics; ConsumerGroup.ipynb demonstrates how multiple consumers coordinate to split partition consumption within a group, a key mechanism for scaling consumption horizontally.
tour.languageLesson: In Kafka's publish/subscribe model, producers append records to a topic's partitions and consumers read them independently at their own pace. A consumer group ensures each partition is read by only one consumer within the group, letting you scale throughput by adding consumers up to the partition count.

tour.title: Closing the Loop: Kafka into Spark Structured Streaming
tour.description: This capstone notebook for the Kafka module connects everything from Steps 7-9: KafkaSpark_StructuredStreaming.ipynb uses Spark's readStream.format('kafka') to turn a Kafka topic directly into a streaming DataFrame, processing the key/value/timestamp records with the same DataFrame operations taught in Step 7. It demonstrates why the course paired Kafka with a Spark cluster rather than a standalone broker -- the whole point is showing event streaming and distributed batch/stream processing as complementary technologies.

tour.title: Dask Module: A Pythonic Alternative to Spark
tour.description: The final module returns to distributed computing with Dask, a lighter-weight, more Pythonic alternative to Spark. dask/docker-compose.yml sets up a scheduler, scalable worker nodes, and a Jupyter client (mirroring the Spark topology from Step 6 but using Dask's own scheduler/worker model), and dask/README.md documents how to scale workers and access the Dask dashboard. This module intentionally revisits concepts from Steps 6-7 -- delayed execution, bags, and dataframes -- so students can directly compare Dask's API ergonomics against PySpark's.

tour.title: Dask: Delayed, Bags, and DataFrames
tour.description: The three Dask lectures mirror the Spark progression from Step 7 but with Dask's API. Lecture1.ipynb covers connecting to the cluster via a Client and basic delayed/submit/map primitives (word count, Fibonacci, computing pi -- the same exercises as PySpark's Lecture1); Lecture2.ipynb introduces Dask Bag, an API analogous to Spark RDDs, with map/filter/pluck/groupby operations; Lecture3.ipynb is the largest notebook in the module, covering dask.dataframe as a partitioned, lazy analogue to Pandas DataFrames, directly paralleling PySpark's DataFrame lecture from Step 7.
tour.languageLesson: Dask's delayed decorator wraps a function call into a lazy task graph node instead of executing it immediately -- the computation only runs when .compute() is called, letting Dask optimize and parallelize the whole graph. Dask DataFrame partitions a large logical DataFrame into many Pandas DataFrames processed independently across workers, the same partitioning idea behind Spark DataFrames but staying closer to native Pandas semantics.
